title: Behavioral Patterns II
summary: Five more behavioral GoF patterns — Iterator, Chain of Responsibility, Mediator, Memento, Visitor — for traversal, delegation, and coordination.

blocks.markdown:
**Behavioral patterns** shape how objects communicate and share responsibility, not how they're built or structured. This topic covers five more from the GoF catalog, continuing from [behavioral-patterns-i](behavioral-patterns-i).

- **Iterator** — walk a collection without exposing its internals.
- **Chain of Responsibility** — pass a request along handlers until one deals with it.
- **Mediator** — centralize how a group of objects talk to each other.
- **Memento** — capture and restore an object's past state.
- **Visitor** — add new operations to a class hierarchy without editing it.

blocks.subTitle: At a glance
blocks.markdown:
What each pattern actually solves.

| Pattern | Solves |
|---|---|
| Iterator | Uniform traversal |
| Chain of Responsibility | Sequential handling |
| Mediator | Many-to-many coupling |
| Memento | Undo / rollback |
| Visitor | New ops, stable classes |

A sixth GoF behavioral pattern, **Interpreter** (defines a grammar and evaluates sentences in it, e.g. rule engines), is rare in interviews — know the name, skip the depth.

blocks.subTitle: Problem & when
blocks.markdown:
**Iterator** gives a way to step through a collection's elements one at a time, without exposing whether it's an array, a tree, or a linked list underneath.

- Problem: client code that loops over a collection gets coupled to its internal structure — swap a list for a tree and every loop breaks.
- The iterator owns a **cursor** (a pointer to "where we are") and exposes just `hasNext()` / `next()`.
- Use when you want one traversal interface across many collection types, or several independent traversals over the same collection at once.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode
blocks.markdown:
```text
interface Iterator:
    method hasNext() -> bool
    method next() -> Item

class ListIterator implements Iterator:
    collection
    cursor = 0

    constructor(collection):
        this.collection = collection

    method hasNext():
        return this.cursor < this.collection.size()

    method next():
        item = this.collection.get(this.cursor)
        this.cursor = this.cursor + 1
        return item

class NameList:
    items = []
    method createIterator():
        return new ListIterator(this)

// client — never touches NameList's internals
iterator = nameList.createIterator()
while iterator.hasNext():
    print(iterator.next())
```

blocks.subTitle: Problem & when
blocks.markdown:
**Chain of Responsibility** passes a request along a line of handler objects until one of them handles it, without the sender knowing which one will.

- Problem: an `if/elif` ladder that checks "can handler A do it? else B? else C?" grows rigid and hard to extend.
- Each handler holds a reference to the **next** handler and either handles the request or forwards it.
- Use for approval flows (manager → director → VP by amount), middleware pipelines, or event bubbling in UIs.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode
blocks.markdown:
```text
abstract class Approver:
    next = null

    method setNext(handler):
        this.next = handler
        return handler

    method handle(amount):
        if this.canApprove(amount):
            print(this.name() + " approved $" + amount)
        else if this.next != null:
            this.next.handle(amount)
        else:
            print("No one could approve $" + amount)

class Manager extends Approver:
    method canApprove(amount): return amount <= 1000
    method name(): return "Manager"

class Director extends Approver:
    method canApprove(amount): return amount <= 10000
    method name(): return "Director"

manager = new Manager()
director = new Director()
manager.setNext(director)

manager.handle(5000)   // forwarded to Director, approved
```

blocks.subTitle: Problem & when
blocks.markdown:
**Mediator** pulls the communication logic between a group of objects into one central object, so those objects no longer reference each other directly.

- Problem: without it, N objects that all need to coordinate end up holding references to every other one — a tangled many-to-many web.
- Colleagues talk **only** to the mediator; the mediator decides who else needs to know.
- Use for chat rooms (each user only knows the room, not every other user), UI forms where one field's change affects several others, or air-traffic-control-style coordination.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode
blocks.markdown:
```text
class ChatRoom:  // the mediator
    method broadcast(sender, message):
        for user in this.users:
            if user != sender:
                user.receive(sender.name, message)

class User:
    room
    name

    constructor(room, name):
        this.room = room
        this.name = name

    method send(message):
        this.room.broadcast(this, message)   // never talks to other Users directly

    method receive(fromName, message):
        print(this.name + " got from " + fromName + ": " + message)

room = new ChatRoom()
alice = new User(room, "Alice")
bob = new User(room, "Bob")
room.users = [alice, bob]

alice.send("hello")   // Bob receives it; Alice never referenced Bob
```

blocks.subTitle: Problem & when
blocks.markdown:
**Memento** captures an object's internal state so it can be restored later, without breaking that object's encapsulation (exposing its private fields to the code that saves the snapshot).

- Three roles: the **originator** (object whose state is saved), the **memento** (an opaque snapshot), and the **caretaker** (holds mementos, never reads them).
- The caretaker stores snapshots blindly; only the originator knows how to read one back.
- Use for undo/redo, save points in games, or rolling back a failed transaction.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode
blocks.markdown:
```text
class Memento:            // opaque snapshot
    state
    constructor(state):
        this.state = state

class Editor:             // originator
    text = ""

    method save() -> Memento:
        return new Memento(this.text)

    method restore(memento):
        this.text = memento.state

class History:            // caretaker — stores, never inspects
    snapshots = []

    method push(memento):
        this.snapshots.append(memento)

    method pop() -> Memento:
        return this.snapshots.removeLast()

editor = new Editor()
history = new History()

editor.text = "draft v1"
history.push(editor.save())
editor.text = "draft v2 (oops)"

editor.restore(history.pop())   // back to "draft v1"
```

blocks.subTitle: Problem & when
blocks.markdown:
**Visitor** lets you add a new operation over a whole class hierarchy without changing any of those classes, by moving the operation into a separate visitor object.

- Problem: adding a method to every class in a hierarchy (e.g. `export()` on every shape) means editing each one, every time you need a new operation.
- Each element exposes `accept(visitor)`, which calls back `visitor.visitShape(this)` — a technique called **double dispatch** (the operation run depends on both the element's type and the visitor's type).
- Use when operations change often but the class hierarchy is stable — e.g. an AST where you add a new pass (print, type-check) without touching node classes.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode
blocks.markdown:
```text
interface Shape:
    method accept(visitor)

class Circle implements Shape:
    radius
    method accept(visitor):
        visitor.visitCircle(this)

class Square implements Shape:
    side
    method accept(visitor):
        visitor.visitSquare(this)

interface Visitor:
    method visitCircle(circle)
    method visitSquare(square)

class AreaVisitor implements Visitor:      // new operation, no Shape edits
    method visitCircle(circle):
        print("area: " + 3.14 * circle.radius * circle.radius)
    method visitSquare(square):
        print("area: " + square.side * square.side)

shapes = [new Circle(2), new Square(3)]
visitor = new AreaVisitor()
for shape in shapes:
    shape.accept(visitor)
```

Common mistakes:

- **Chain with no end.** Forgetting a fallback handler (or a cycle in the chain) means a request silently vanishes or loops forever.
- **Fat mediator.** Piling all coordination logic into one Mediator turns it into a god object — split by concern if it grows large.
- **Leaky memento.** Letting the caretaker read or modify memento internals breaks encapsulation — it should only store and hand back the opaque object.
- **Visitor forcing a public API.** Visitor needs elements to expose enough state for the visitor to act on, which can pressure you into loosening encapsulation.

blocks.subTitle: Iterator's purpose
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What problem does Iterator solve, and where have you seen it?**

It separates *how you traverse* a collection from *how the collection is built*, so client code loops the same way whether the data is an array, tree, or hash map. Every `for-each` loop over a list, and language-level iterators like Java's `Iterator` or Python's `__iter__`, are Iterator in production.

blocks.subTitle: Chain of Responsibility, real use
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is Chain of Responsibility, and give a real use case?**

A request is passed along a sequence of handlers until one handles it, so the sender doesn't need to know which handler will act. Real use: HTTP middleware pipelines (auth, logging, rate-limit, then route handler), where each layer either processes the request or forwards it to the next.

blocks.subTitle: What Mediator solves
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What problem does Mediator solve?**

It removes direct references between a group of collaborating objects by routing all communication through one central mediator. Instead of N objects each knowing about every other, each knows only the mediator — cutting many-to-many coupling down to one-to-many.

blocks.subTitle: When to use Memento
blocks.markdown:
**Q: When would you reach for Memento?**

When you need undo/redo, save points, or rollback, and want to snapshot an object's state without exposing its internals to whoever stores the snapshot. The caretaker holding the history never inspects or edits a memento — only the originator that created it knows how to read one back.

blocks.subTitle: What problem Visitor solves
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What problem does Visitor solve, and what's double dispatch?**

It lets you add new operations over a stable class hierarchy without touching those classes — the operation lives in a visitor instead. Double dispatch means the method that actually runs depends on two types: the element's (via `accept`) and the visitor's (via `visitX`) — needed because most languages only dispatch on one type at a time.
